source.title: Constructing groups of 'small' order: Recent results and open problems

accepted.question_text: Let L_n denote a set containing one representative of each isomorphism type of finite group of order n, so |L_n| is the number of isomorphism types of groups of order n. Is there a closed formula for |L_n|, or a general method that determines |L_n| for arbitrary n without explicitly listing all groups?
accepted.context_brief: Counting groups of a given order

accepted.question_text: Let L_n denote the isomorphism types of finite groups of order n. For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 20000 such that 2^10 divides n or 3^9 divides n, can L_n be completely enumerated, including both nilpotent and non-nilpotent groups? These are the orders in the source's case E1, where the obstruction is the very large number of p-groups already present at orders 2^10 and 3^9.

Let E2 be the set of integers n with 1 <= n <= 20000 for which 2^9 * p is a proper divisor of n for some p in {3, 5, 7}. For the 18 orders in E2, can the finite groups of order n be enumerated up to isomorphism despite the large number of groups already occurring at each base order 2^9 * p?

Let E3 be the set of integers n with 1 <= n <= 20000 such that 2^8 * p^2 divides n for p in {3, 5, 7}. For the orders in E3 other than the already determined exception n = 2^8 * 3^2 = 2304, can the solvable finite groups of order n be constructed or enumerated up to isomorphism, possibly by improving the Frattini extension method?

For the six exceptional orders n = 8748 = 2^2 * 3^7, 10368 = 2^7 * 3^4, 13122 = 2 * 3^8, 16000 = 2^7 * 5^3, 17496 = 2^3 * 3^7, and 18816 = 2^7 * 3 * 7^2, can the finite groups of each order be constructed up to isomorphism, including determining the missing solvable groups while keeping the known nilpotent counts and known non-solvable counts fixed?

For each of the 34 orders at most 20000 for which the number of finite groups has been enumerated but the groups themselves have not been explicitly constructed, can one construct representative groups for every isomorphism type? The orders include 2^10; the 32 orders of the forms 2^9 * p for odd prime p, 2^8 * p * q for p in {3, 5, 7} and q prime different from 2 and p, 2^7 * 3^2 * p for p prime different from 2 and 3, and the specific orders 8640, 9600, 13440, 16320, 17280, 19440; and the additional order 12500.

Can the remaining small-order group enumerations that lack an independent verification be cross-checked by a second method? The unresolved reliability target consists of six non-solvable cases that were not cross-checked and, on the solvable side, 183 orders below 20000 for which the solvable groups were enumerated by only one method, while another 39 orders still remained open for enumeration.
accepted.context_brief: Independent verification of computed group data

trace.notes: Normalized the single input URL https://zbmath.org/6980605 as a zbMATH resolver record. Direct shell fetch of the zbMATH page returned a Cloudflare challenge, so the zbMATH API was used only to identify the exact work, title, authors, DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-70566-8_8, year 2017, and article pages 199-211.

Exact-title recovery found the author-hosted PDF https://www.quendi.de/data/papers/EHH2018-small-groups.pdf. Its visible title matches the zbMATH record title, so it was selected as the readable primary source. A shell curl download attempt for this PDF failed with local DNS resolution for www.quendi.de, but the PDF was readable through the page-reading tool and used as the extraction artifact.

Mapped the PDF structure: Section 1 introduces L_n and the lack of a closed formula; Sections 2-5 describe enumeration and construction algorithms and GAP data; Section 6 is titled Open cases and challenges and contains the main unresolved enumeration and construction cases; Section 7 discusses reliability and remaining cross-check gaps.
Extracted the introduction's explicit statement that no closed formula is known for the group-counting function |L_n|.
Extracted Section 6.1 case E1: orders up to 20000 divisible by 2^10 or 3^9 remain infeasible enumeration targets.
Extracted Section 6.1 case E2: orders with proper divisor 2^9 * p for p in {3, 5, 7} remain infeasible enumeration targets.
Extracted Section 6.1 case E3: orders divisible by 2^8 * p^2 for p in {3, 5, 7} are difficult Frattini-extension construction cases; n = 2304 is explicitly marked as the solved exception.
Extracted the six exceptional orders whose group construction is explicitly called an open problem.
Extracted Section 6.2's construction challenge for 34 orders where only enumeration counts, not explicit group constructions, are available.
Extracted Section 7's implicit reliability challenge: some enumerations have not been independently cross-checked and many solvable-order computations used only one method.
Expanded L_n into a standalone definition and rewrote the source statement as a closed-form counting question.
Expanded E1 into its divisibility condition and made the target complete enumeration of finite groups up to isomorphism.
Expanded E2 into its proper-divisor condition and prime set.
Expanded E3 into its divisibility condition, stated the solved exception n = 2304, and limited the question to the remaining construction/enumeration challenge.
Inlined the six exceptional orders and their prime decompositions from the source table.
Expanded the 34 known-count-only construction problem by spelling out the order families and explicit listed orders.
Rewrote the reliability gap as a self-contained independent-verification question and included both non-solvable and solvable-side quantities.
No near-duplicate found; retained as the general counting-function problem.
Kept distinct from E2, E3, and exceptional-order cases because it is defined by different divisibility conditions.
Kept distinct from E1, E3, and exceptional-order cases because it is defined by a proper-divisor condition involving 2^9 * p.
Kept distinct because it concerns the E3 Frattini-extension construction difficulty and excludes the solved n = 2304 case.
Kept distinct because the six exceptional orders are explicitly outside E1, E2, and E3.
Kept distinct because it concerns explicit construction for orders whose counts are already known, not enumeration of unknown counts.
Kept distinct because it is a verification challenge rather than an enumeration or construction target.
